tip: 'Se faire avoir' is literally 'to get oneself had' – the set phrase for being tricked or scammed: 'je me suis fait avoir' = I got taken in, I fell for it.
'Avant que' can add an optional 'ne' with no negative meaning: 'avant qu'il ne parte' = before he leaves.
'Faillir' + verb means to nearly do something: 'avait failli avoir un accident' = had almost had a crash. This verb basically only lives in past tenses.
'Bien que' (although) always forces the subjunctive: 'bien que le temps fût'. That 'fût' is the literary imperfect subjunctive of 'être' – in speech you'd just say 'soit'.
'Faire' + infinitive means having something done: 'faire construire' = to have built. The subject causes the action, someone else does it.
Very informal: 'ça craint' = that sucks. Slang, never use in formal contexts.
'Poser un lapin' is literally 'to place a rabbit', but it means to stand someone up. 'Il m'a posé un lapin' = he no-showed and left me waiting. No rabbit involved.
Saying you don't believe something triggers the subjunctive: 'je ne crois pas qu'il ait raison' takes 'ait', not 'a'.
'Se faire la malle' literally means 'pack your trunk' – slang for clearing off suddenly: 'il s'est fait la malle' = he ran off.
In reported speech 'qu'est-ce que' becomes 'ce que': 'Qu'est-ce que tu penses ?' turns into 'ce que je pensais'.
Informal: 't'inquiète' = 'ne t'inquiète pas' with both 'ne' and 'pas' dropped – very common in casual speech.
'Insister' needs 'pour' before 'que', where English expects a plain 'that': 'insister pour que nous partions' – and 'partions' is subjunctive.
'Que ce soit clair' = 'let it be clear'. Starting a sentence with 'que' + subjunctive ('soit') states a wish or order, where English uses 'let' or 'may'.
Informal: 'avoir la classe' = to look cool, and 'costard' is slang for 'costume' (suit).
'Concours' normally means a competition or contest – but in formal French it means help or support. 'Votre concours' here is your assistance, not a contest.
'Ce n'est pas tant... que' means 'it's not so much... as': here, not so much the price as the lack of quality.
'Un froid de canard' = 'bitter cold'. Origin: duck hunting in winter.
'Il semble que' + subjunctive (uncertainty): 'que ce soit vrai'. 'Il me semble que' + indicative (more certain).
'Ménager la chèvre et le chou' is literally 'spare the goat and the cabbage' – feed the goat without letting it eat the cabbage. Means please both sides.
After a superlative, French usually switches to the subjunctive: 'le plus beau... que j'aie jamais vu' takes 'aie', not 'ai'. Same after 'seul', 'premier', 'dernier'.
'Tourner autour du pot' is literally 'circling around the pot', where English beats around the bush – both mean stalling instead of getting to the point.
'Mettre son grain de sel' is literally 'to add your grain of salt' – but it means butting in with an unasked opinion, not the English skepticism sense.
'Quoi que' (two words) + subjunctive = whatever. Don't confuse with 'quoique' (one word) = although.
Asking 'crois-tu que...?' can trigger the subjunctive when doubt is implied: 'crois-tu qu'il soit capable', with 'soit' instead of 'est'.
'Il est dommage que' + subjunctive: regret/judgment triggers subjunctive.
'Il est peu probable que' + subjunctive: low probability triggers subjunctive.
'Tout brillant qu'il soit' = 'however brilliant he may be'. 'Tout' + adjective + 'que' takes the subjunctive ('soit') to concede a point.
'Nous avons le plaisir de' = we are pleased to. Standard business/formal announcement opening.
'Pied-à-terre' = a second home, usually small, in another city.
Informal: 'grave' alone = 'totally/absolutely'. Youth slang.
